description: The physics behind datacenter power and cooling: energy, thermodynamics, entropy and Landauer, heat transfer, chip power scaling and facility metrics. For architects who need to reason about density, cooling and energy from first principles.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: What is energy, in the most useful one-line sense?
notes.back: A quantity that stays constant over time in an isolated system. It changes form (electrical, chemical, kinetic, heat) but the total is fixed. Unit: joule (J).
notes.analogy: A fixed pile of coins moved between pockets. A datacenter moves coins from the 'electricity' pocket to the 'heat' pocket, doing something useful on the way.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: Why is energy conserved at all?
notes.back: Because the laws of physics are the same at every moment. Time-translation symmetry ⇒ energy conservation (Noether's theorem): each symmetry of the laws gives a conserved quantity.
notes.analogy: Energy is the bookkeeping that time-symmetry forces on nature.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: Energy vs power?
notes.back: Energy = amount, in joules. Power = rate of flow, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Energy = power × time.
notes.analogy: Energy is the water in the bucket, power is how fast the tap runs. Bills are for the bucket; capacity planning is for the tap.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.extra: So: a 1 MW datacenter running one hour uses 1 MWh = 3.6 GJ.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: Where does all the electrical energy that enters a datacenter end up?
notes.back: As heat inside the building, watt for watt in steady state (only a negligible sliver leaves as light in fibres or radio).
notes.analogy: Computation doesn't consume energy, it degrades it: high-grade electricity in, low-grade warm air out.
notes.extra: Consequence: cooling must be sized for the full IT load. Every watt you power, you must also remove.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: Electrical power in terms of voltage and current?
notes.back: P = V × I (watts = volts × amperes).
notes.extra: Why it matters: the same power can be delivered at high V / low I (low losses) or low V / high I (high I²R losses).

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::01 Energy & Power
notes.front: 'Race to idle': why can a faster, hungrier chip use less total energy?
notes.back: Energy = power × time. Drawing 2× the power but finishing in ⅓ of the time uses ⅔ of the energy, then the chip drops to low-power idle. What counts is joules per job.
notes.extra: Condition: only works if idle power is genuinely low.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics make possible?
notes.back: If A is in equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is with C. That makes temperature well-defined: the thing that's equal when two bodies stop exchanging net heat. A thermometer is just body B.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: First law of thermodynamics (words and formula)?
notes.back: Energy is conserved: ΔE = Q − W, the change in internal energy = heat added − work done by the system.
notes.extra: Server in steady state: electrical work in = heat out, ΔE = 0.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: Second law of thermodynamics, in its most practical form?
notes.back: Total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. So heat flows spontaneously only hot → cold, heat can't be fully turned into work, and cooling below ambient costs work.
notes.analogy: You can't unshuffle a deck by shaking it. A chiller fights this drift, and the second law sets its minimum price.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: Heat vs temperature?
notes.back: Heat: energy in transit because of a temperature difference (J). Temperature: how concentrated the energy is per degree of freedom (K). The ocean holds lots of heat at low temperature.
notes.extra: DC angle: 40 °C exhaust carries many kW but sits only a little above room temperature, so it's hard to use.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: Why can't you cool a server room below ambient 'for free'?
notes.back: Heat only flows on its own from hot to cold. Moving it from a cool room to warmer outside air needs a heat pump (chiller), which consumes work.
notes.analogy: Pumping water uphill: possible, but you pay for every metre of lift. The lift is the inside–outside temperature difference.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.text: Carnot limit for a heat engine: η<sub>max</sub> = {{c1::1 − T<sub>cold</sub>/T<sub>hot</sub>}} (in kelvin).
notes.extra: Example: 40 °C exhaust to a 20 °C environment: at most 1 − 293/313 ≈ 6% recoverable as work. That's why waste heat can't economically become electricity.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.text: Chiller COP = {{c1::heat removed / work spent}}. Carnot maximum: COP<sub>max</sub> = {{c2::T<sub>cold</sub> / (T<sub>hot</sub> − T<sub>cold</sub>)}} (kelvin); real chillers reach ~30–60% of it.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: Carnot COP for cooling to 20 °C (293 K) with 35 °C (308 K) outside?
notes.back: COPmax = 293 / 15 ≈ 19.5. Real chillers manage ~5–8 here.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::02 Laws of Thermodynamics
notes.front: What is exergy, and why is server exhaust heat 'low-quality'?
notes.back: Exergy = the part of energy that can still do useful work given the surroundings. Heat near ambient temperature has almost none, even in megawatts.
notes.analogy: Energy is conserved, exergy is not: a datacenter turns high-exergy electricity into near-zero-exergy warm air.
notes.extra: Heat reuse: district heating needs a heat pump to lift it to 60–70 °C; efficient at modest ΔT, but never free.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why does heat capacity decide air vs liquid cooling?
notes.back: Per unit volume, water carries ~3500× more heat per kelvin than air. Removing the same heat with the same temperature rise takes ~3500× more volume of air.
notes.extra: Then: at some kW per rack the airflow (and fan power) needed becomes absurd; that's where liquid stops being optional.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.text: Water carries ~3500× more heat per m³·K than air. Volumetric heat capacity: water ≈ {{c1::4.2 MJ/(m³·K)}}; air ≈ {{c2::1.2 kJ/(m³·K)}}.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.text: Heat carried by a fluid stream: Q = {{c1::ṁ · c<sub>p</sub> · ΔT}} (mass flow × specific heat × temperature rise). Twice the heat at the same ΔT needs {{c2::twice the flow}}.
notes.analogy: The fluid is a conveyor belt for heat: belt speed × load per kilogram × how much warmer you let it get.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Fourier's law of conduction, and its electrical analogy?
notes.back: Q = k·A·ΔT/L. Like Ohm's law: ΔT plays voltage, heat flow plays current, and thermal resistance = L/(k·A).
notes.extra: So: thin, wide, copper paths pass heat; thick, narrow, insulating ones resist it. A heat sink is a low thermal resistance.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Thermal resistance chain: how do you get the chip junction temperature?
notes.back: Resistances in series add: Tjunction = Tair + Q × (Rpackage + Rpaste + Rsink + …).
notes.extra: Example: 300 W through 0.2 K/W total sits 60 K above the air. Raise inlet air and the whole chain shifts up.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Newton's law of cooling (convection): what are the knobs?
notes.back: Q = h·A·(T<sub>surface</sub> − T<sub>fluid</sub>). More area (fins), a better or faster fluid (higher h), or a larger ΔT.
notes.extra: Why inlet temperature matters: warmer incoming air shrinks ΔT, so you need more area or airflow for the same heat.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why does raising the allowed server inlet temperature save chiller energy?
notes.back: A higher T<sub>cold</sub> shrinks the temperature lift, which raises COP: every joule moves more heat.
notes.extra: Trade-off: hotter chips leak more and server fans spin faster.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why does a chiller's Coefficient of Performance (COP) fall when the outside air gets hotter?
notes.back: Carnot COP = T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold). A hotter outside raises the denominator (a bigger temperature lift), so each joule of work moves less heat.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Besides better COP, what second saving does a warmer inlet set-point unlock?
notes.back: More hours per year when outside air is cooler than the set-point, so free cooling (economisers, no compressor) can do the job.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why is evaporative cooling so effective, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Latent heat: evaporating 1 kg of water absorbs ≈2260 kJ, as much as heating 540 kg of water by 1 K. It cools air without a compressor but consumes water.
notes.extra: Trade-off: cheap in electricity, expensive in water; behind the datacenter water-use debate.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why doesn't a datacenter overheat instantly when cooling fails?
notes.back: Thermal mass: air, metal and loop water store heat, so temperature rises at heat load ÷ total heat capacity. For dense racks that ride-through may be only seconds to minutes.
notes.analogy: A bathtub: a big tub fills slowly. A chilled-water tank is a deliberately bigger tub to cover generator start-up.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Square–cube law: why is heat removal a surface problem?
notes.back: Grow an object by L and its volume (heat generated) grows as L³ but its surface (heat escape) only as L². Denser and bigger things overheat more easily.
notes.analogy: Elephants have big ears, chips have fins, racks have fans: all add surface to something that has outgrown its own.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Fan (and pump) affinity laws: how do airflow, pressure and power scale with speed?
notes.back: Airflow ∝ speed, pressure ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³. Doubling airflow costs 8× the fan power.
notes.extra: Why liquid wins at density: it needs ~3500× less volume flow, so pumping power stays small.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Fan speed is cut by 20%. Roughly what happens to airflow and fan power?
notes.back: Airflow falls 20%, but power ∝ speed³ so it falls to 0.8³ ≈ 0.51, i.e. about half. Small airflow cuts save large amounts of fan power.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::03 Heat Transfer & Cooling
notes.front: Why are rising rack densities pushing datacenters to liquid cooling?
notes.back: Racks went from ~5 kW to 40–130+ kW. Air carries little heat per m³ and fan power grows with the cube of airflow, so air becomes impractical; water carries ~3500× more per m³ for little pumping power.
notes.extra: Three facts stack: denser chips (Dennard breakdown), a poor heat carrier (air), cubic fan cost.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: What is entropy, in the statistical-mechanics sense?
notes.back: The logarithm of the number of microstates consistent with what you know: S = k ln Ω. It measures ignorance of the fine detail, not 'disorder' as such.
notes.analogy: A shuffled deck isn't physically different from a sorted one; you just know less. 'Shuffled' allows 52! orders, 'sorted' allows 1.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: Why is entropy defined with a logarithm?
notes.back: Independent systems combine as Ω₁ × Ω₂ states, and ln(Ω₁Ω₂) = ln Ω₁ + ln Ω₂. The log makes entropy additive, like energy.
notes.analogy: Counts multiply, logs add: two bytes have 256 × 256 states but 8 + 8 = 16 bits.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: What is Boltzmann's constant k, physically?
notes.back: A conversion factor between temperature and energy (≈1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J/K). kT is the typical thermal energy per degree of freedom, and it sets the size of thermal noise.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.text: At room temperature (300 K), kT ≈ {{c1::4.1 × 10<sup>−21</sup> J}} ≈ {{c2::0.026 eV (≈ 1/40 eV)}}.
notes.extra: Use: energy barriers ≫ kT are safe from thermal noise; transistor thresholds are only ~10–20 kT, so voltage can't shrink much further.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: How is temperature defined via entropy (statistical mechanics)?
notes.back: 1/T = dS/dE: temperature is the inverse of how much entropy a system gains per unit of energy added. Cold bodies gain a lot per joule; hot ones little.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: Using dS/dE, why does heat flow from hot to cold?
notes.back: Moving a joule from hot (small dS/dE) to cold (large dS/dE) loses a little entropy and gains more, so total entropy rises. The reverse would lower it: not forbidden, just astronomically unlikely.
notes.analogy: Energy flows to whoever 'appreciates' an extra joule most, and cold bodies appreciate it more.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: Is the second law strict or statistical?
notes.back: Statistical. The microscopic laws are reversible and conserve information; entropy rises because we track only coarse averages. A decrease is allowed, just too improbable to ever see in large systems.
notes.analogy: Every collision could run backwards, but a shuffled deck sorting itself needs every shuffle to go 'right'.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: Boltzmann distribution: how likely is a state with energy E at temperature T?
notes.back: Probability ∝ e<sup>−E/kT</sup>. States far above kT are exponentially rare: one kT up is ~37% as likely, ten kT up ~0.005%.
notes.extra: Why it matters: stored bits and transistor states stay stable only while their energy barriers are many kT high.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: What does equipartition say, and what does it imply for heat capacity?
notes.back: In equilibrium each independent way of storing energy (degree of freedom) holds ½ kT on average. More ways to 'wiggle' per unit volume → higher heat capacity.
notes.analogy: Heating fills every available pocket a little; water has many pockets per m³, air few and sparse.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: What is the relationship between Shannon entropy and thermodynamic entropy, and what does one bit correspond to?
notes.back: Same formula, −Σ p ln p, different units (bits vs J/K). One bit of uncertainty = k ln 2 J/K of thermodynamic entropy.
notes.extra: Bridge: k ln 2 turns a bit into a physical quantity, which is what makes computing thermodynamic.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: Landauer's principle: why must erasing a bit release heat?
notes.back: Erasing takes the memory from 2 possible states to 1, lowering its entropy by k ln 2. The second law requires at least that much entropy, kT ln 2 of heat, to go into the surroundings.
notes.analogy: Information is physical because forgetting is physical.
notes.extra: Scope: applies to logically irreversible operations (erase, AND, OR); reversible ones need not pay.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.text: Landauer limit at 300 K: kT ln 2 ≈ {{c1::2.9 × 10<sup>−21</sup> J}} per bit erased.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: How far above the Landauer limit is real hardware, and so what limits computing energy today?
notes.back: A transistor switch costs ~10−18–10−17 J and a full operation with data movement ~10−12–10−10 J, so 10³–10⁸× above the floor. Engineering limits energy (capacitance, voltage, wires, leakage), not fundamental physics.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::04 Entropy & Information
notes.front: What is reversible computing, and why is it thermodynamically interesting?
notes.back: Computing only with logically reversible gates (output determines input) erases nothing, so in principle it pays no Landauer cost; only the final reset does.
notes.extra: Lesson: the energy of computing is about erasure, not 'thinking'. Practical hardware is still far from competitive.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.text: CMOS dynamic power: P ≈ {{c1::α · C · V² · f}}, where α = fraction of transistors switching per cycle, C = switched capacitance, V = supply voltage, f = clock frequency.
notes.analogy: Each switch charges a tiny capacitor (½CV²) and dumps it as heat, f times a second.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Why does supply voltage matter more than frequency for chip power?
notes.back: P ∝ V²f, and lowering V also forces lower f (f ∝ V), so P ∝ V³. A 10% voltage cut saves ~19% at fixed f, and ~27% once f drops with it.
notes.extra: Hence: DVFS, undervolting, and many slower cores beating one fast core per watt.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: What is leakage (static) power, and why is it thermally dangerous?
notes.back: Current through transistors that aren't switching. It grows exponentially with temperature, so hotter → more leakage → more heat: positive feedback that can run away.
notes.extra: Upside: better cooling directly lowers chip power (a Boltzmann-factor effect on your bill).

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Why does better cooling reduce a chip's power draw, not just its temperature?
notes.back: Leakage power grows exponentially with temperature. A cooler die leaks less, so it draws less power for the same work, and the feedback loop runs in the good direction.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: What was Dennard scaling?
notes.back: Shrink a transistor by s and you can also cut voltage by s and raise frequency by s while power density stays constant. For ~30 years, more transistors came with free speed and no extra cooling.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Why did Dennard scaling break down around 2005?
notes.back: Voltage stopped scaling: below ~1 V, leakage explodes because transistors need thresholds well above kT. With V stuck, packing in more transistors raises power density.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: What did the end of Dennard scaling cause?
notes.back: Clock speeds plateaued at ~3–5 GHz, the industry moved to multicore, and 'dark silicon' appeared: parts of a chip that can't all be powered at once.
notes.extra: For datacenters: power density (100+ W/cm²) made them cooling problems first.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Moore's law vs Koomey's law?
notes.back:
Moore: transistors per chip double ~every 2 years.
Koomey: computations per joule doubled ~every 1.5 years until ~2000, now ~every 2.5–3 years.
notes.extra: DC angle: if demand grows faster than Koomey efficiency, total energy rises; the current AI situation.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Why does moving data cost more energy than computing on it?
notes.back: Wires are capacitors: each bit charges a wire, costing ∝ C·V², and C grows with length. A flop costs ~pJ; fetching its operand from DRAM ~100–1000× more.
notes.analogy: Distance = capacitance = energy.
notes.extra: Hence: caches, near-memory compute, HBM, and GPU focus on bandwidth per watt.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: How does chip power density compare with everyday hot things?
notes.back: Server CPU/GPU dies run ~50–150 W/cm², versus ~5–10 W/cm² for a kitchen hotplate and ~100 W/cm² for a nuclear reactor core.
notes.extra: Hence: the die-to-coolant thermal path must be very short; liquid moves onto the package.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: Amdahl's law: what caps parallel speedup?
notes.back: With parallel fraction p on N processors, speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N), so never more than 1/(1 − p). A 95%-parallel job tops out at 20×.
notes.extra: Link: Dennard's end forced multicore; Amdahl caps what multicore buys.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::05 Chip Power & Scaling
notes.front: A job is 90% parallel. What speedup do 1000 processors give, and what does that say about buying more processors?
notes.back: Speedup = 1/(0.1 + 0.9/1000) ≈ 9.9×. The serial 10% dominates, so beyond a few dozen processors extra hardware mostly adds power and cost, not speed.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: Why does power distribution use higher voltages (48 V racks, HVDC)?
notes.back: Conductor loss = I²R. For fixed P = V·I, doubling V halves I and cuts losses to a quarter.
notes.analogy: Current is what heats wires; voltage just rides along.
notes.extra: But: every conversion step loses a few percent, so the number of steps matters too.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: Rack power rises from 10 kW to 100 kW at the same voltage and the same cables. What happens to resistive loss in the cables, and why?
notes.back: Current rises 10× (I = P/V), so loss I²R rises 100×. That is why high power density forces higher voltage or thicker conductors.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE): definition and typical values?
notes.back: PUE = total facility energy / IT equipment energy. 1.0 is ideal; modern hyperscale ~1.1; legacy rooms 1.5–2.0.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: A facility has Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) 1.2 and an Information Technology (IT) load of 10 MW. What is the total power draw, and how much heat must be removed in steady state?
notes.back: Total = 1.2 × 10 = 12 MW. All of it ends up as heat, so the cooling plant must remove 12 MW, not just the 10 MW of IT load.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: What is PUE's blind spot?
notes.back: It measures overhead, not usefulness: it says nothing about whether the IT energy does useful work. Idle servers with great cooling score a great PUE.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: Why is energy per useful operation the right efficiency metric?
notes.back: You pay for joules and must remove joules as heat. J/op = W ÷ (op/s). Improve it with fewer joules per switch (voltage, capacitance) or fewer switches per result (algorithms, less data movement).

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: How does the speed of light constrain datacenter and network design?
notes.back: Signals travel ~20 cm/ns in fibre or copper (≈5 ns per metre, ⅔ of c). 100 m ≥ 0.5 µs one way; 1000 km ≥ 5 ms one way. No engineering removes it.
notes.analogy: Latency budgets are distance budgets.
notes.extra: Hence: memory millimetres from compute, short-cable topologies, regional cloud footprints.

notes.deck: Physics for Datacenters::06 Facility Scaling & Metrics
notes.front: Why can synchronous replication of every write between datacenters 1000 km apart not be fast, whatever the engineering?
notes.back: A round trip needs at least 2 × 5 ms = 10 ms because signals travel at ~⅔ c in fibre. Each synchronous commit waits at least that long, so distance sets a latency floor.
